The 5-Minute Website Audit: 15 Quick Checks Every Contractor Should Do Monthly

Quick 5-minute website audit for contractors. 15 checks to ensure your site is generating leads. Free audit tool included.

OnwardCraft Team Growth Strategists

Your website is your hardest-working employee. It never sleeps, never takes a vacation, and it is the first impression most potential customers have of your business. But here is the problem: most contractor websites have silent issues that are costing them leads every single day. A broken form, a slow-loading page, or a phone number that does not click to call on mobile can mean the difference between a $15,000 roofing job and a prospect calling your competitor instead.

The good news? You do not need to be a web developer or hire an expensive agency to catch these problems. In fact, you can run a comprehensive contractor website audit in just five minutes. This is not a deep technical dive into server logs or JavaScript minification. This is a practical, contractor-focused website health check designed to catch the issues that actually matter for lead generation. The kind of problems that make homeowners bounce before they ever fill out a quote request.

Think of this quick website audit as your monthly maintenance routine, similar to checking your work truck before heading to a job site. You would not drive to a customer’s house with a flat tire or a broken ladder rack. Your website deserves the same attention. By setting aside just five minutes each month to run through these 15 checks, you will catch problems early, protect your lead flow, and ensure your digital storefront is always open for business.

Whether you are a plumber, HVAC technician, electrician, roofer, or general contractor, this monthly website check is built specifically for your business. Each check includes exactly what to look for, why it matters for your bottom line, and how to fix common issues. Let us get started.

How to Use This Audit

Before diving into the 15 checks, here is how to get the most out of this process. Set a recurring calendar reminder for the first Monday of every month. Block off five minutes, grab your phone and your laptop, and work through each check systematically. Some checks require you to view your site on a mobile device, while others are best done from a desktop. Keep a simple spreadsheet or notebook where you track your findings month over month. If something was broken last month and is still broken this month, that is a red flag that needs immediate attention.

The goal is not perfection on the first pass. The goal is consistency. A website that is checked monthly and fixed quickly will outperform a "perfect" site that is neglected for six months. Now, let us walk through each of the 15 checks.

Check 1: Is Your Phone Number Clickable?

What to Look For

Open your website on your smartphone. Navigate to your homepage, your services page, and your contact page. Tap your phone number. Does it automatically open your phone app with the number pre-filled? Or does nothing happen? A clickable phone number uses a "tel:" link in the HTML code behind your site. When coded correctly, tapping the number triggers an immediate call option.

Why This Matters

Over 60 percent of local service searches happen on mobile devices. When a homeowner has a burst pipe at 10 PM or an AC unit that died during a heatwave, they are not going to copy and paste your number into their dialer. They are going to tap and call. If your number is not clickable, you are creating friction at the exact moment when a prospect is ready to buy. That friction sends them straight to a competitor whose site works properly.

This is especially critical for emergency services. Plumbers, HVAC companies, and electricians who offer 24/7 emergency repair cannot afford to lose a single call because of a non-clickable number. Every missed tap is a missed opportunity for a high-margin emergency job.

How to Fix It

If your phone number is plain text, ask your web developer or website platform to wrap it in a tel: link. The code looks like this: <a href="tel:+1234567890">(123) 456-7890</a>. Most modern website builders like WordPress, Wix, Squarespace, and Webflow support this natively. If you are using a WordPress page builder, there is usually a "link" option where you can enter "tel:your-number" instead of a web URL.

Test this on both iPhone and Android, as they handle tel: links slightly differently. Also, make sure your number appears above the fold on mobile, meaning a visitor does not have to scroll to find it. The best practice is to place a sticky header or prominent call button that stays visible as users scroll.

Check 2: Do Your Forms Work?

What to Look For

Go to your main contact form or quote request form. Fill it out completely using a test name, email, and phone number. Click submit. Did you receive a confirmation message on the screen? Did you receive an email notification? Check your spam folder. Now try submitting the form with a required field left blank. Does it show a clear error message? Test this on both desktop and mobile.

Why This Matters

Form failures are one of the most common and most expensive website problems for contractors. A broken form is a silent killer because you often do not know it is broken until a customer calls to complain that you never responded to their quote request. By then, you have already lost their trust and their business.

Many contractors rely on contact forms as their primary lead capture method. If your form is not delivering submissions to your inbox, you might as well not have a website. Even worse, some forms appear to submit but the backend email system fails, giving you a false sense of security. This is why testing must be done actively, not assumed.

How to Fix It

If your form is not working, start by checking your form plugin or platform settings. In WordPress, popular form plugins like WPForms, Gravity Forms, and Contact Form 7 have email notification settings that can break when hosting changes occur. Verify that the "To" email address is correct and that notifications are not being filtered by spam.

Consider adding a backup notification method. Many form plugins allow you to send submissions to multiple email addresses or integrate with CRMs like HubSpot, Zoho, or JobNimbus. This creates redundancy so a single email failure does not cost you a lead. Also, add a simple thank-you page redirect after form submission instead of just an on-screen message. This gives you a clear confirmation and allows you to track conversions in Google Analytics.

Check 3: Is Your Site Loading Fast?

What to Look For

Open your homepage in an incognito or private browser window. Time how long it takes for the page to fully load. Does the main content appear within two seconds? Do images pop in quickly, or do they load slowly and push text around? You can also use free tools like Google PageSpeed Insights or GTmetrix to get an objective score. Pay attention to both mobile and desktop scores.

Why This Matters

Speed is not just a technical vanity metric. It directly impacts your lead generation. Google research shows that 53 percent of mobile users abandon a site that takes longer than three seconds to load. For contractors, this means a slow site is actively driving potential customers away before they ever see your services, your reviews, or your contact information.

Speed also affects your search rankings. Google uses page speed as a ranking factor, especially for mobile search. If your competitor’s site loads in one second and yours takes five, Google is more likely to show their site above yours in search results. For local contractors competing in crowded markets, every ranking position matters.

How to Fix It

Start by compressing your images. Most contractor websites are slow because of oversized photos from job sites. Use a tool like TinyPNG or ShortPixel to reduce image file sizes without losing quality. If you are on WordPress, install a caching plugin like WP Rocket or W3 Total Cache. These plugins create static versions of your pages so they load faster for repeat visitors.

Minimize the number of plugins and third-party scripts on your site. Every Facebook pixel, chat widget, and analytics tool adds load time. Only keep the ones you actively use. If your hosting is cheap shared hosting, consider upgrading to managed WordPress hosting or a VPS. The investment pays for itself if it prevents even one lost lead per month.

Check 4: Is Your Site Mobile Responsive?

What to Look For

Pull up your website on your smartphone. Does the text fit the screen without requiring horizontal scrolling? Are buttons large enough to tap with a thumb? Do images resize properly, or do they overflow the screen? Navigate through your services pages, your about page, and your contact page. Check that your navigation menu works smoothly on mobile. Some sites use "hamburger" menus that fail to open or display incorrectly on certain devices.

Why This Matters

Google has been using mobile-first indexing since 2019, meaning it primarily uses the mobile version of your site for ranking and indexing. If your site does not function well on mobile, you are not just frustrating users, you are telling Google that your site is lower quality than competitors who have invested in responsive design.

For contractors, mobile responsiveness is non-negotiable. Your customers are often searching while dealing with an urgent home issue. They are standing in a flooded basement or a freezing living room, using their phone to find help fast. A site that requires pinching, zooming, or scrolling sideways adds stress to an already stressful situation. They will leave and call the next contractor on the list.

How to Fix It

If your site is not mobile-friendly, the fix depends on your platform. Most modern WordPress themes are responsive by default, but older custom themes may need updates. Test your site using Google’s Mobile-Friendly Test tool for specific issues. Common problems include text that is too small, content wider than the screen, and clickable elements placed too close together.

Ensure your tap targets, buttons and links, are at least 48 pixels tall and wide. This is the minimum recommended size for comfortable thumb tapping. Avoid using pop-ups that cover the entire screen on mobile, as these are penalized by Google and frustrate users. If you need a complete redesign, prioritize a mobile-first approach where the mobile experience is designed first and the desktop experience follows.

Check 5: Are Your CTAs Visible?

What to Look For

A CTA, or call-to-action, is any element that prompts a visitor to take the next step. This could be a "Get a Free Quote" button, a "Call Now" link, or a "Schedule Service" form. Look at your homepage, services pages, and blog posts. Can you find a clear CTA within three seconds of landing on each page? Are the buttons a contrasting color that stands out from the rest of the design? Do they use action-oriented language like "Call Now" instead of passive language like "Contact Us"?

Why This Matters

Your website exists to generate leads. Every page should guide visitors toward contacting you. If your CTAs are buried at the bottom of long pages, use bland colors that blend into the background, or use vague language, you are leaving money on the table. Visitors do not hunt for ways to contact you. You must make it obvious and easy.

Contractor websites often make the mistake of treating CTAs as an afterthought. They spend hours perfecting service descriptions but use a tiny text link at the bottom of the page for contact. The most successful contractor sites repeat their primary CTA multiple times per page: once above the fold, once after explaining the service, and once at the bottom. This redundancy increases conversion rates because it catches visitors at different stages of readiness.

How to Fix It

Use a contrasting color for your CTA buttons. If your site uses blue and white, make your CTA buttons orange or green. The color should draw the eye without clashing. Use first-person language where possible. "Get My Free Estimate" converts better than "Get a Free Estimate" because it feels more personal.

Place your primary CTA in your website header so it is visible on every page. Many contractors use a sticky header with a "Call Now" or "Get a Quote" button that stays at the top of the screen as users scroll. Test different CTA placements and language using simple A/B tests if your platform supports it. Even small changes like switching from "Submit" to "Send My Quote" can increase form submissions by 10 to 20 percent.

Check 6: Are Reviews Displayed?

What to Look For

Scroll through your homepage and key service pages. Do you see customer reviews or testimonials? Are they recent, within the last six months? Do they include the customer’s name and location for credibility? Are they pulled from Google, or are they generic text that could have been written by anyone? Check if you have a dedicated reviews or testimonials page.

Why This Matters

Reviews are social proof, and social proof drives conversions. According to BrightLocal, 87 percent of consumers read online reviews for local businesses before making a purchase decision. For contractors, where jobs often cost thousands of dollars, trust is everything. A homeowner is not going to let a stranger into their house and hand over a deposit without confidence that you deliver quality work.

Displaying reviews directly on your website keeps visitors engaged instead of sending them away to Google or Yelp where they might get distracted or see a competitor. It also reinforces the positive impression they may have already formed from seeing your Google reviews. Fresh, recent reviews signal that your business is active and consistently delivering great service.

How to Fix It

If you do not have reviews on your site, start by embedding your Google Business Profile reviews. Google provides a free widget that displays your latest reviews with real names and star ratings. There are also WordPress plugins like "Widget for Google Reviews" or "TrustIndex" that pull reviews automatically and keep them updated.

Create a testimonials page that showcases your best reviews organized by service type. A homeowner looking for roof repair wants to see roof-specific reviews, not just generic praise. Include photos of completed projects next to relevant testimonials when possible. This combination of visual proof and verbal praise is incredibly persuasive. If your reviews are outdated, implement a review request system. Send a follow-up text or email three to five days after job completion asking satisfied customers to leave a review.

Check 7: Is Your Google Business Profile Linked?

What to Look For

Find the footer of your website and your contact page. Do you see a link to your Google Business Profile, often labeled as "Find Us on Google" or "View Our Google Reviews"? Click the link. Does it go to the correct GBP page? Is the link visible and easy to find, or is it hidden among dozens of other footer links?

Why This Matters

Your Google Business Profile is often the first thing potential customers see when they search for your services. It appears in Google Maps, local search results, and the local pack. Linking to it from your website creates a powerful two-way signal: your website validates your GBP, and your GBP validates your website. This consistency strengthens your local SEO and helps Google understand that your business is legitimate and active.

For contractors, the GBP is especially important because it displays your reviews, photos, business hours, and service areas directly in search results. Many homeowners will visit your GBP before they ever click through to your website. Making it easy for website visitors to find and interact with your GBP increases engagement signals that Google uses for ranking.

How to Fix It

Add a prominent link to your GBP in your website footer, on your contact page, and in your header if space allows. Use the direct URL to your GBP, which you can find by searching your business on Google Maps and copying the share link. Do not use a redirect or a shortened URL.

Consider adding a Google review badge or button that links directly to your review form. This makes it easy for satisfied customers to leave reviews and shows prospects that you are confident in your reputation. If you have multiple locations, link each location page on your website to its corresponding GBP. This local-specific linking helps each location rank in its service area.

Check 8: Are Your Photos Current?

What to Look For

Browse through your website’s photo gallery, homepage banner, and service pages. Are the photos from recent jobs, or are they from five years ago? Do they show modern equipment, current branding on your trucks, and up-to-date uniforms? Are the images high quality, well-lit, and professional? Check if you have any placeholder images or stock photos that do not represent your actual work.

Why This Matters

Photos are the closest thing to a showroom for contractors. Homeowners want to see the quality of your work before they invite you into their home. Outdated photos suggest that your business is stagnant or that you are not actively taking on new projects. Low-quality or generic stock photos destroy trust because they signal that you either do not have real work to show or do not care enough to present it well.

Current photos also help with local SEO. Google can read image filenames and alt text, so photos named "roof-replacement-phoenix-2025.jpg" with descriptive alt text send strong local relevance signals. Fresh photos on your GBP and website show Google that your business is active, which can improve your visibility in local search.

How to Fix It

Make it a habit to take photos at every job site. Before, during, and after shots are gold for contractor marketing. Train your crew leads to snap a few high-quality photos with their smartphones at the start and end of each project. Most modern phones take excellent photos if you follow basic principles: shoot in good light, keep the horizon level, and focus on the work, not the background clutter.

Update your website gallery at least quarterly. Replace the oldest photos with new ones, and rotate your homepage banner image to showcase recent projects. Add descriptive filenames and alt text to every image. Instead of "IMG_1234.jpg," use "emergency-plumbing-repair-dallas-tx.jpg." This small step improves both SEO and accessibility.

Check 9: Is Your Contact Information Correct?

What to Look For

Verify your business name, phone number, email address, and physical or service area address on every page where it appears. Check your website footer, contact page, about page, and any location-specific pages. Does the information match exactly what is on your Google Business Profile, Yelp, Facebook, and other directory listings? Even small differences like "St." versus "Street" or suite number placement can cause problems.

Why This Matters

Inconsistent contact information across the web is one of the fastest ways to confuse both customers and search engines. When Google sees different versions of your NAP, name, address, and phone number, it loses confidence in your business data. This confusion can lower your local search rankings and cause your GBP to display incorrect information.

For customers, inconsistent information creates frustration and doubt. If your website shows one phone number and your GBP shows another, which one is correct? If your address is outdated, will the customer show up at the wrong location? These small inconsistencies erode trust and can lead to missed calls, missed appointments, and negative reviews.

How to Fix It

Create a single document with your official business name, address, phone number, and email. Use this exact format everywhere. Update your website first, then systematically update your GBP, Yelp, Facebook, BBB, and all other directory listings. Tools like Moz Local, BrightLocal, or Yext can help you manage and sync your listings across dozens of platforms.

If you have moved, changed phone numbers, or rebranded, prioritize updating your NAP everywhere as soon as possible. The longer inconsistencies persist, the more they hurt your SEO and confuse potential customers. Set a calendar reminder to verify your contact information quarterly as part of this monthly website check.

Check 10: Is Your SSL Certificate Active?

What to Look For

Look at the URL bar in your browser when visiting your website. Do you see a padlock icon next to your URL? Does the URL start with "https://" or just "http://"? Click on the padlock icon and check the certificate details. Is it valid and current? Does it match your domain name exactly? Test this on multiple pages, not just your homepage.

Why This Matters

An SSL certificate encrypts data transmitted between your website and your visitors. Without it, any information submitted through your contact forms, including names, addresses, and phone numbers, is sent in plain text and can be intercepted. Browsers like Chrome and Safari now display a "Not Secure" warning for sites without SSL, which immediately scares away visitors.

For contractors, SSL is especially important because you collect sensitive lead information. Homeowners submitting quote requests are trusting you with their personal details. A "Not Secure" warning makes your business look unprofessional and untrustworthy. Google also uses SSL as a ranking signal, so a missing certificate can hurt your search visibility.

How to Fix It

Most modern web hosting providers offer free SSL certificates through Let’s Encrypt. If your site is not using HTTPS, contact your hosting provider and ask them to install an SSL certificate. This is usually a quick, free process. Once installed, update your website settings to force all traffic to the HTTPS version of your site.

After installing SSL, check for mixed content warnings. These occur when your site loads some resources, like images or scripts, over HTTP instead of HTTPS. Mixed content can break the padlock icon and trigger browser warnings. Use a tool like Why No Padlock to identify and fix mixed content issues. Set a reminder to check your SSL expiration date annually, though most modern certificates auto-renew.

Check 11: Are Your Links Working?

What to Look For

Click through the main navigation menu on your website. Does every link go to the correct page? Check your footer links, sidebar links, and any links within your page content. Pay special attention to links to external sites like manufacturer pages, industry associations, or partner businesses. Do any links lead to 404 error pages or redirect to unrelated sites?

Why This Matters

Broken links create a poor user experience and signal neglect. When a visitor clicks a link expecting to learn more about your HVAC maintenance plans and lands on a 404 error page, they assume your site is outdated or poorly maintained. This erodes trust and increases bounce rates, both of which can hurt your SEO.

External links that redirect to spam sites or unrelated content are even worse. If your site was hacked or an external site you linked to was sold and repurposed, those links can damage your reputation and potentially trigger security warnings from Google. Regular link checks protect both your users and your search rankings.

How to Fix It

For a quick manual check, click through your main navigation and footer links once per month. For a more thorough check, use a free broken link checker tool like Dead Link Checker or the Broken Link Checker plugin for WordPress. These tools crawl your entire site and report any broken or redirected links.

Fix broken internal links by updating them to the correct page URL. If a page no longer exists, redirect the old URL to a relevant replacement page using a 301 redirect. For broken external links, either remove the link or replace it with a link to a current, relevant resource. Make link checking part of your regular website performance check routine.

Check 12: Is Your Content Current?

What to Look For

Read through your homepage headline and main service descriptions. Do they reflect your current service offerings? Check your blog posts. When was the last one published? Is your "About" page still accurate regarding your team size, years in business, and service areas? Look for any seasonal promotions, outdated pricing, or references to old equipment models or discontinued services.

Why This Matters

Stale content suggests that your business is inactive or out of touch. If your last blog post is from 2021 and your homepage still advertises a 2022 promotion, visitors will wonder if you are still in business. Fresh, updated content signals professionalism and keeps visitors engaged longer, which improves your search rankings.

Current content also helps you rank for seasonal and trending searches. An HVAC company that updates its content to address summer heatwaves or winter freeze warnings will capture more search traffic than a competitor with static, year-old pages. For contractors, content freshness is a competitive advantage.

How to Fix It

Update your homepage headline and main service descriptions at least twice per year. Add a blog post or news update at least once per month. Even a short post about a recent project, a seasonal maintenance tip, or a new service offering keeps your site active. If you do not have time to blog, consider adding a "Recent Projects" or "Latest News" section that is easier to maintain.

Review your service pages quarterly to ensure accuracy. Remove discontinued services, update pricing language, and refresh any outdated technical information. If you serve new areas or have added new team members, update your about and location pages immediately. The goal is to ensure that every piece of information on your site is accurate and current.

Check 13: Is Your Chat Working?

What to Look For

If you have a live chat widget or chatbot on your website, open your site in a private browser window. Does the chat widget appear? Can you initiate a conversation? If you send a test message, does it reach the intended recipient, whether that is an email, a CRM, or a live chat dashboard? Check if the chat widget loads properly on mobile devices and does not cover important content.

Why This Matters

Live chat has become an expected feature for service businesses. Many homeowners, especially younger demographics, prefer texting or chatting over calling. A broken or missing chat widget means you are missing leads from an entire segment of your market. Even worse, a chat widget that appears but does not deliver messages creates false hope and frustration.

Chat also provides a competitive advantage. If a homeowner is comparing three HVAC companies and yours is the only one with instant chat availability, you are more likely to capture that lead. Chat transcripts also give you valuable data about common customer questions, which can inform your content and sales strategy.

How to Fix It

Test your chat widget monthly by sending a test message from an incognito window. Verify that notifications are reaching the right person or team. If you use a chatbot, review the conversation flows to ensure they still make sense and guide users toward booking a call or submitting a form.

If you do not have live chat, consider adding one. Tools like Tidio, LiveChat, and Drift offer affordable plans for small businesses. Many integrate with Facebook Messenger, allowing you to manage website chat and social media messages in one place. Set clear expectations for response times, and if you cannot offer 24/7 chat, use an away message that tells visitors when they can expect a reply and offers alternative contact methods.

Check 14: Is Emergency Messaging Visible?

What to Look For

If your business offers emergency services, check that this is prominently displayed on your homepage and contact page. Is there a clear "24/7 Emergency Service" banner or badge? Can visitors find your emergency phone number within seconds of landing on your site? Check if your emergency messaging is visible on mobile, where urgent searches most often happen.

Why This Matters

Emergency services are high-margin jobs for contractors. A burst pipe at midnight or a furnace failure on a subzero night is not a price-sensitive situation. The homeowner needs help fast, and they will call the first contractor who looks available and capable. If your emergency services are buried on an interior page or not mentioned at all, you are invisible to these high-value leads.

Emergency messaging also builds trust with non-emergency visitors. Seeing that you offer 24/7 service signals that you are a serious, established business with the capacity to handle urgent situations. This reassurance can influence their decision even if they are just scheduling routine maintenance.

How to Fix It

Add an emergency service banner to the top of your homepage. Use urgent colors like red or orange and action-oriented language like "Call Now for 24/7 Emergency Service." Make the phone number clickable and place it in your sticky header so it is always visible. Create a dedicated emergency services page that explains what constitutes an emergency, your response time, and your service area.

If you offer different emergency numbers for after-hours calls, make sure those numbers are correct and routed properly. Test your after-hours answering service or on-call rotation monthly to ensure calls are being answered. Nothing destroys trust faster than an emergency number that goes to voicemail.

Check 15: Is Your Tracking Working?

What to Look For

Check if Google Analytics 4 is installed on your website. You can verify this by installing the Google Tag Assistant browser extension or by viewing your site’s source code and searching for "G-" or "UA-" tracking IDs. Log into your Google Analytics account and check if data is being collected. Are you seeing recent visitor activity? Do your traffic numbers make sense, or are they suspiciously low or high?

Also check if you have conversion tracking set up. Are form submissions, phone calls, and chat interactions being recorded as conversions? If you run Google Ads, is your conversion pixel firing correctly? Look at your Google Search Console account to verify that your site is indexed and receiving impressions.

Why This Matters

Tracking is how you know if your website is working. Without accurate data, you are flying blind. You cannot tell which marketing channels are driving leads, which pages are converting, or where visitors are dropping off. This makes it impossible to optimize your site or allocate your marketing budget effectively.

For contractors, tracking is especially important because leads come through multiple channels: phone calls, form submissions, chat messages, and direct emails. If you are only tracking form submissions, you are missing the majority of your lead data. Proper tracking gives you a complete picture of your website’s performance and ROI.

How to Fix It

If you do not have Google Analytics 4 installed, install it immediately. GA4 is the current standard and replaces the old Universal Analytics. Set up conversion events for every lead action on your site: form submissions, phone number clicks, email link clicks, and chat initiations. Use Google Tag Manager to manage all your tracking codes in one place.

Set up Google Search Console and verify ownership of your website. This free tool shows you which search queries are driving traffic, your average position, and any indexing issues. Review your analytics dashboard weekly, not just monthly, so you can spot trends and anomalies quickly. If your traffic drops suddenly, it could indicate a technical problem, a Google algorithm update, or a tracking issue that needs immediate attention.

Your Monthly Website Audit Scorecard

To make this quick website audit even easier, use this simple scorecard each month. Give yourself one point for each check that passes. Aim for 15 out of 15 every month.

Check Pass / Fail Notes
1. Phone number clickable
2. Forms working
3. Site loading fast
4. Mobile responsive
5. CTAs visible
6. Reviews displayed
7. GBP linked
8. Photos current
9. Contact info correct
10. SSL active
11. Links working
12. Content current
13. Chat working
14. Emergency messaging visible
15. Tracking working

Score: ___ / 15

If you score below 12, prioritize fixing the failed checks before the end of the week. If you score below 10, consider your website at risk of losing leads and schedule time for immediate repairs.

When to Call in the Pros

This contractor website audit is designed to catch the most common lead-killing issues quickly. But it is not a substitute for a comprehensive professional audit. If you find multiple failed checks month after month, or if your site has deeper issues like poor search rankings, low traffic, or outdated design, it is time to bring in experts.

A professional website audit goes beyond these surface checks. It includes technical SEO analysis, conversion rate optimization, user experience testing, competitive analysis, and a strategic roadmap for improvement. Think of this monthly check as changing your oil, and a professional audit as a full engine diagnostic.

Conclusion

Your website should be your most reliable source of leads. By running this 5-minute website audit every month, you will catch small problems before they become expensive disasters. You will keep your site fast, functional, and trustworthy. And you will ensure that every visitor who finds you online has a smooth path to becoming a paying customer.

The contractors who win in today’s market are not necessarily the ones with the biggest budgets or the flashiest sites. They are the ones who pay attention to the details. A clickable phone number, a working form, a fast-loading page, these small things add up to a big competitive advantage.

Set your calendar reminder now. Block off five minutes on the first Monday of every month. Work through these 15 checks, record your score, and fix anything that is broken. Your future customers, and your bottom line, will thank you.
